title: The scout
hook: a long portrait of the Cynic as scout and witness, sent to report what's really good

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was alone, which isn't the same as forlorn. Your line was someone you can live with is there.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU CAN LIVE WITH IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Before an ancient army moved, it sent a few people ahead. They slipped into the hills, looked at the ground, counted the campfires across the valley, and came back to say what was really there. Everything hung on that report. A scout who panicked and said a thousand enemies when there were ten could send a whole army running from nothing. Epictetus loved this picture. In one of the longest talks in the Discourses, book three, chapter twenty-two, he uses it to describe a certain kind of philosopher.
screen: `SENT AHEAD INTO THE HILLS.` → `COUNT THE FIRES. COME BACK.` → `THE SCOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the Cynics: a Greek movement usually traced back more than four centuries before Epictetus, to Diogenes of Sinope, who lived on almost nothing: a rough cloak, a bag, a staff, and a large storage jar to sleep in. Their name most likely comes from kyon, Greek for dog. It seems to have started as an insult, and they wore it on purpose. Then the scout. The true Cynic, Epictetus says, is sent ahead to find out what is friendly to human beings and what is hostile, and to come back and report it truthfully. Not frightened or dazzled into a false one. The report: people hunt for happiness where it isn't, in money, office and others' good opinion, and it lives in their own choices. Most of that long chapter is a warning. A young man asks about taking up the Cynic life, and Epictetus tells him, in effect, don't you dare do it lightly. The cloak and staff are the easy part. The real Cynic has nothing to hide, keeps his mind clean, takes a beating without hating the one who gives it, and cares for everyone like a father or a brother. In book one, Epictetus says Diogenes was sent out as a scout and came back with a calm report: death is no evil, because it isn't shameful. Elsewhere he calls the philosopher a witness, whose own life shows you can lose what the world prizes and still be well. You don't need a cloak for the small version. A scout simply looks at what's there and says so.
screen: `THE CYNICS: NAMED FOR THE DOG.` · `SENT AHEAD TO SEE WHAT IS GOOD.` · `A WARNING: NOT A COSTUME.` · `A WITNESS WHO REPORTS PLAINLY.` · then, large: `A SCOUT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you'll report on today, how a meeting went, how a parent sounded on the phone, and notice the report you'd usually give, shaped by worry or by wanting to look good. Then ask slowly: what did I actually see, and what did I add? Hold only the plain report, the ten fires, no more and no less.
The scout. Epictetus' picture of the philosopher sent ahead to see what is truly good and bad, and to come back and report it honestly, without fear. Today's word.
Your line: a scout. Report what you saw, with nothing added and nothing hidden. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often try to separate what happened from what they added to it, and to describe events to others plainly, the way Epictetus' scout reports the ground.

chat.says: Why did Epictetus call a philosopher a scout?
options: A scout goes ahead, sees what's truly good or bad, and reports it honestly.
A scout roams with a cloak and staff, showing everyone how tough he is.
A scout spies on other people and reports their faults to the crowd.
chat.meaning: Epictetus says the true Cynic is sent ahead like a scout to learn what helps and harms people, then report it truthfully, not frightened or dazzled.

Cynics.meaning: Greek philosophers who lived on almost nothing; likely named for dogs

Diogenes of Sinope.meaning: the Cynic who lived on almost nothing and slept in a jar

Discourses.meaning: Arrian's record of Epictetus' talks, in four books

notes: Discourses 3.22.23–25: the Cynic as a scout (kataskopos) sent to learn what is friendly and hostile to people and report truthfully; paraphrased. Confirm the chapter location of the scout image (it also appears in 1.24.3–10).
Discourses 1.24: Diogenes sent as a scout reports that death is no evil, since it is not shameful; paraphrased. Confirm.

'Witness' (martys): Epictetus calls the philosopher a witness called by God in 1.29.46–49; the index pairs scout and witness for 3.22. The script says 'elsewhere he calls the philosopher a witness' to avoid placing it in 3.22. Confirm.

Diogenes' storage jar (pithos) is from Diogenes Laertius 6.23; the Cynic name from kyon, dog, is standard but its exact origin is debated (some link it to the Cynosarges gymnasium where Antisthenes taught). The teach now says 'most likely' and 'seems to have'.
Founder of the Cynics is debated: ancient sources name Antisthenes, a student of Socrates, as well as Diogenes; the script says the movement is 'usually traced back' to Diogenes. Confirm.
'More than four centuries before Epictetus': Diogenes c. 412/404–323 BCE; Epictetus c. 50–135 CE.
The 3.22 portrait (nothing to hide, beaten and loving the one who beats him, father and brother to all) is paraphrased; confirm the summary is fair.
